claims.text: Cauchy introduced the general method for resolving systems of simultaneous equations on 18 October 1847, and Hadamard later named the procedure the method of descent.

source.title: Cauchy, A. L., Méthode générale pour la résolution des systèmes d’équations simultanées, Comptes Rendus de l’Académie des Sciences, Paris, 25:536-538, 1847

claims.text: The origin is layered rather than single: steepest descent is traced to Cauchy in 1829 for a nonlinear equation, Curry published on the non-linear minimization case in 1944, and Kantorovich introduced the form in use today in 1945.

source.title: Cauchy, A. L., Méthode générale pour la résolution des systèmes d’équations simultanées, Comptes Rendus de l’Académie des Sciences, Paris, 25:536-538, 1847

claims.text: The ordinary notion of distance used when saying a direction is steepest is the Euclidean one, in which moving one unit along any axis costs the same — a property of the coordinates chosen rather than of the function being optimised.

source.title: Cauchy, A. L., Méthode générale pour la résolution des systèmes d’équations simultanées, Comptes Rendus 25:536-538, 1847

beats.broke: in one dimension there are two directions and the slope picks one, and in many dimensions there are infinitely many directions and no single number can choose
beats.fix: collect the slope along each axis into a vector, whose direction is the one in which the function increases fastest
beats.cost: fastest is measured against a notion of distance you never stated, so rescaling an input changes which direction counts as steepest
beats.interview: why rescaling your inputs changes the path that gradient descent takes
